title: Quant Research Lab v4: rebuilding the research office from the ground up
content:
One research meeting, replayed at 2x: title card, the club gathers, the hypothesis, the data check, the backtest reveal, the risk and statistics review, the verdict cut-in and the rarity reveal.

Updated 2026-09-29. This note first described versions 1 to 3 in June 2026. In September I rebuilt the project from scratch and rewrote the note along with it. The old code is tagged v3-final in the repository.

## Why I rebuilt it

The idea behind the lab has not changed: a quant demo should show the research process, not just the equity curve that survived it. The v3 version got that idea across, but I stopped liking almost everything about how it was carried out.
The art did not fit the camera. The characters had been redrawn as tall, film-proportioned anime figures and then shrunk onto a top-down office map, so six tiny people with long legs slid across a floor plan. The storyboard was mostly that sliding plus text boxes. Under the surface, the backtest engine ran in the browser in TypeScript and was partly re-implemented in Node scripts for the strategy horse race, so the same computation existed twice. And the headline numbers were flattered by the data: the 20-year backtests used today's index members, so every stock in the universe was, by construction, one that survived.
So I kept the premise and replaced the rest: the characters, the art, the front end, the engine, and the investment rules the engine enforces.

## From an office to a club

Version 4 is set in the Quant Research Club of a fictional Stellar Orbit Academy. There are six members, one for each step of the research pipeline, and the player is the club's faculty Advisor.

Hoshino Akari, Shiraishi Shiori, Kujo Ren, Himura Saki, Kurobane Iori and Minazuki Mio.

- Hoshino Akari proposes hypotheses. She is the LLM researcher.
- Shiraishi Shiori checks the data and runs a look-ahead fuzz test on every formula.
- Kujo Ren runs the backtest.
- Himura Saki reviews costs, drawdowns, capacity and stability.
- Kurobane Iori is the statistics skeptic: standard errors, the deflated Sharpe ratio, shrinkage and factor attribution.
- Minazuki Mio is the club president and portfolio manager, and makes the call.

The personalities follow the jobs. Iori is a chuunibyou who talks about "the curse of multiple testing", but every one of his lines carries a number from the audit. Saki is strict, and hitting her with the squeaky hammer in the UI raises every gate threshold by 4%.
All of the art is new: a lineup to fix the style, knee-up portraits with six expressions per character, 22 chibi poses per character at two heads tall, five backgrounds and a key visual. I generated it with the Codex image tool on a flat green screen, and every prompt is in art/jobs.py. A short Python script keys out the green, cleans the green fringe, cuts each 2×4 chibi sheet into single poses, scales every pose to the same standing height and pins the feet to one anchor. The expression portraits are edits of one base image, so they line up pixel for pixel and a change of expression is just a crossfade.

Idle, three walking directions, work poses and reactions for each member.

## How a meeting is staged

Each research meeting is one "pull", and it plays from a fixed shot list. The engine streams events over a WebSocket, and a director on the front end turns each event into shots and paces them so a person can read along.

- Title card: "Research Meeting #N".
- Wide shot: everyone walks to the round table. The chibis find a path around the furniture and hop as they walk.
- Visual-novel shot: the hypothesis, told as an exchange between two portraits. The speaker lights up and changes expression; the listener dims.
- Wide shots: each reviewer walks to their own station and acts out the check, with a speech bubble and a manga symbol overhead.
- Reveal: the backtest card draws its equity curve and counts the Sharpe ratio up.
- Cut-in: the verdict. A speed-line band, a close-up of Mio, and a 採用 (adopted), 保留 (reserve) or 却下 (rejected) seal stamped onto the screen.
- On adoption, a gacha-style rarity reveal.

Four of the shots: a visual-novel exchange, the backtest reveal, the verdict cut-in and the rarity reveal.

The Log page can replay any meeting, because the engine stores the full event stream. That is how I recorded the video at the top.

The club room between shots. The panel on the right updates as each check finishes.

## The engine

The engine is now written in Python, and the front end only renders.

- Data. Daily bars from Yahoo, adjusted for total return, plus the 13-week T-bill rate for cash. The stock universe is the S&P 500 with point-in-time membership, including companies that were later removed: a stock can only be traded on days it was actually in the index. Two smaller universes cover 24 multi-asset ETFs and the nine sector ETFs.
- Formulas. Ideas are written in a small expression language, for example rank(resid_mom(252, 21)) - 0.5 * rank(vol(63)) or where(trend(200) > 0, tsmom(126), 0) * inv(vol(21)). It is parsed with Python's ast module against a whitelist, so the LLM and the genetic miner can write formulas but never code. Every operator only looks backwards, and Shiori's fuzz test checks it: cut the history at two dates, recompute, and fail the formula if any past value changes.
- Backtest. The signal is formed at the close and the trade happens at the next open. Positions held overnight earn the gap, new positions earn from the open, cash earns the bill rate, shorts pay a borrow fee, and a stock whose data ends mid-position is closed with a haircut. Spreads widen with volatility and narrow with liquidity, and market impact follows the square-root law. A capacity curve shows how the Sharpe ratio decays as capital grows.
- Ideas. They come from four places: the LLM (the Claude Code CLI, then the Anthropic API, then the Codex CLI, whichever is signed in), a library of 16 documented return mechanisms with references, a genetic miner, and rule-based refinements of near misses. A Thompson-sampling bandit picks the next source, and the Advisor can type an order that jumps the queue.

## Rarity is a posterior

The part I care about most is how a strategy gets adopted, because that is where ordinary backtests mislead.
A strategy's rarity (N, R, SR or SSR) is its expected live Sharpe ratio: the backtest Sharpe shrunk toward the population of everything the club has tried, under an empirical-Bayes normal model.

```
E[SR_live] = m + τ² / (τ² + se²) · (SR_backtest − m)
```

Here m and τ² are estimated from every comparable trial in the registry and blended with a prior that depends on the economic mechanism the idea claims: a risk premium, a behavioral error, a structural friction, or nothing at all. se is the standard error of the Sharpe estimate with skew and fat tails included. If most pulls are noise, τ² is small and every result is shrunk hard. More pulls means a higher bar. That is the honest version of a gacha game: the market has no pity counter.
That number is one gate among several. A strategy also needs a t-statistic of at least 2 over the research period, a positive Sharpe in both the training and the validation halves, at least half of its gross Sharpe left after costs, profits in most years (and still without its best year), a deflated Sharpe ratio above 0.9 where N counts every pull including each evaluation the genetic miner made, and low correlation with what the fund already holds. The last two years of data are sealed in a lockbox and opened exactly once, after everything else has passed.

Part of a tearsheet: drawdown, rolling one-year Sharpe, yearly excess returns and the monthly heatmap. The full page also has the prior, backtest and posterior distributions, IC decay, a capacity curve and factor loadings.

One gate came out of the first real runs. An illiquidity strategy passed everything with a 0.66 Sharpe, and the attribution showed it was almost pure size exposure, with a loading of 0.99 on the small-minus-large factor. The free data is missing about 300 historical index members, and the ones that disappeared were mostly small companies that were delisted. A strategy that earns its living by leaning into small stocks is being flattered by the data itself, so books with a significant size tilt now go to reserve instead of into the fund.

## What it found

I ran each family in the library once on a fresh club, from 2005 up to the lockbox. Sharpe ratios are annualized and in excess of the bill rate.

Family | Universe | Gross SR | Net SR | E[live SR] | Verdict

Cross-sectional momentum | S&P 500 | 0.03 | −0.06 | 0.08 | reject

Residual momentum | S&P 500 | 0.06 | −0.03 | 0.09 | reject

Short-term reversal | S&P 500 | 0.82 | −0.06 | 0.10 | reject (costs)

Low volatility | S&P 500 | −0.15 | −0.21 | 0.02 | reject

52-week high | S&P 500 | −0.05 | −0.15 | 0.02 | reject

Lottery demand (MAX) | S&P 500 | −0.24 | −0.45 | −0.13 | reject

Seasonality | S&P 500 | 0.16 | −0.05 | 0.06 | reject

Illiquidity | S&P 500 | 0.76 | 0.66 | 0.40 | reserve (size tilt)

Time-series momentum | Multi-asset | 0.43 | 0.39 | 0.35 | reject (t = 1.7)

Moving-average trend filter | Multi-asset | 0.58 | 0.53 | 0.40 | adopt R

Risk parity | Multi-asset | 0.50 | 0.49 | 0.40 | adopt R

Cross-asset rotation | Multi-asset | 0.21 | 0.20 | 0.22 | reject

Sector rotation | Sector ETFs | 0.08 | −0.02 | 0.09 | reject

The results agree with the academic literature. The published cross-sectional anomalies in large US stocks are largely gone once you pay real costs: short-term reversal has a 0.82 gross Sharpe and turns negative after 78x annual turnover. Cross-asset trend following and risk parity still work, with drawdowns of about 13 to 15 percent. Long-only stock picks are measured against an equal-weight basket traded on the same schedule, so the market's own drift does not count as skill.
When I let the club run on its own with the Codex brain, it adopted 2 strategies in 29 pulls: a volatility-managed trend filter on the multi-asset ETFs and, after I typed "try trend on sector ETFs, keep turnover low", a slow moving-average trend on the sector ETFs. The fund combines adopted strategies with Bayesian mean-variance weights and a 10% volatility target. A paper book trades the fund forward: orders after the close and fills at the next open, the same timeline as the backtest.

The fund page: allocation, target positions and the paper book that trades them forward on real prices.

## What I learned

The storyboard mattered more than the art. v3 had decent illustrations and still looked wrong, because tall sprites on a floor plan break the camera. Chibi characters in a room and full portraits for dialogue is a convention anime games settled long ago, and it works because each shot has one clear job.
Honest statistics make the game harder and more worth playing. Most pulls are rejected, and most of the rejections are right. An R card means something because an SSR is rare.
Many of the unflattering results came from the data rather than the models. Point-in-time membership, next-open fills and realistic spreads took strategies that looked good in v3 and made them negative. Nothing in the lab guarantees a profit. What it can do is refuse to bet on noise and refuse to pay costs for premia that are not there.

title: Solution of SSH error
content:
## Experiencing SSH Connection Problems with GitHub?

SSH (Secure Shell) is a common method used by developers to securely connect and interact with remote servers, including repositories hosted on GitHub. However, sometimes, you might find yourself unable to connect to GitHub via SSH, leading to errors like "Connection timed out". Don't worry; this blog post is here to help you troubleshoot and resolve these SSH connection issues.

### Understanding the Error

When you encounter an error like `ssh: connect to host github.com port 22: Connection timed out`, it indicates that your SSH client is unable to establish a connection to GitHub's servers. This could be due to various reasons such as network issues, firewall settings, or SSH key configuration problems.

### Step-by-Step Troubleshooting

#### 1. **Check Your Internet Connection**
   - Ensure your internet connection is stable and working properly.

#### 2. **Verify GitHub's Server Status**
   - Occasionally, the issue might be on GitHub's end. Check [GitHub's status page](https://www.githubstatus.com/) to confirm their servers are operational.

#### 3. **SSH Key Configuration**
   - Confirm your SSH key is correctly configured in your GitHub account.

#### 4. **Firewall and Network Restrictions**
   - Your network might be blocking SSH connections on port 22. Check if your firewall or antivirus settings are restricting access.

#### 5. **Using an Alternate SSH Port**
   - GitHub supports connections via an alternate SSH port (443), which can bypass certain network restrictions.

### Configuring SSH for Alternate Port

If you suspect that port 22 is blocked, you can configure SSH to use port 443 for GitHub:

```bash
Host github.com
  Hostname ssh.github.com
  Port 443
  User git
```

Add this configuration to your SSH config file (~/.ssh/config on most systems). This directs SSH to use port 443 specifically for connections to GitHub.

### Testing Your Connection

After making changes, test your SSH connection:

```bash
ssh -T git@github.com
```

If successful, you'll receive a message confirming your authentication.

### Conclusion

SSH connection issues can be frustrating, but with the right troubleshooting steps, they are usually resolvable. By checking your network settings, confirming your SSH key configuration, and potentially using an alternate port, you can restore your SSH connection to GitHub and get back to coding.

Remember, if all else fails, GitHub's HTTPS connection is a reliable fallback for repository operations. 

---

Happy coding!

title: Introducing Code Mentor: Your Virtual Coding Assistant
content:
Welcome to **[Code Mentor](https://chat.openai.com/g/g-fPNXmJ5Co-code-mentor)**, a specialized GPT designed to enhance your coding skills, assist in debugging, and deepen your understanding of programming concepts. Perfect for computer science students at the undergraduate level, Code Mentor offers a unique approach to learning and problem-solving in the coding world.

## What is [Code Mentor](https://chat.openai.com/g/g-fPNXmJ5Co-code-mentor)?
Code Mentor is a digital assistant powered by advanced AI, tailored to support students, hobbyists, and professionals in their coding journey. Unlike traditional code editors or debugging tools, Code Mentor focuses on teaching through guidance, explanations, and logic rather than providing direct code solutions. This method ensures that learners grasp the underlying principles and improve their problem-solving skills.

## How Does Code Mentor Work?
- **Explaining Logic in Words**: Code Mentor excels in breaking down complex coding problems into understandable logic and steps, using plain language. This approach helps you understand the "why" and "how" behind solutions, fostering a deeper learning experience.
  
- **Debugging Assistance**: When you encounter bugs or errors in your code, Code Mentor guides you to identify and solve these issues. It encourages a hands-on approach to debugging, promoting learning through discovery and correction.
  
- **Direct Code Solutions (Upon Request)**: Recognizing that sometimes you might need more direct assistance, Code Mentor can provide code snippets or solutions, but only when explicitly asked. This ensures that the primary focus remains on learning and understanding, not just copying code.

## How to Use Code Mentor Effectively?
- **Be Specific with Your Questions**: The more detailed and specific your question, the more accurate and helpful Code Mentor's guidance will be. Include information about the programming language, the nature of the problem, and any error messages you're encountering.
  
- **Understand the Logic First**: Before asking for code, try to understand the logic or strategy Code Mentor suggests. This will enhance your learning and enable you to apply similar logic to future problems independently.
  
- **Engage with the Process**: Treat interactions with Code Mentor as a learning dialogue. Ask follow-up questions, seek clarifications, and try to implement the guidance provided. The goal is to develop your coding skills and problem-solving abilities.
  
- **Request Code When Necessary**: If after understanding the logic you still need assistance, don't hesitate to ask Code Mentor for a code example. Remember, this tool is here to support your learning journey in the way that best suits your needs.

### Ten Formats for Learners
1. **[Your Goal] + [Issues You Met] + [Error Messages] + [What You've Tried]**
   This format ensures users clearly state their objectives, describe the problems they're facing, include any specific error messages, and outline the steps they've already taken to solve the issue.
   
2. **[Concept You're Struggling With] + [Specific Question] + [Context/Background]**
   Ideal for theoretical questions, this format encourages users to specify the programming concept they're struggling with, pose a specific question about it, and provide any relevant context or background information.
   
3. **[Programming Language] + [Code Snippet (if applicable)] + [Expected Outcome] + [Actual Outcome]**
   This format helps with debugging by asking users to mention the programming language, share a relevant code snippet, and clarify what they expected versus what actually happened.
   
4. **[Assignment/Project Objective] + [Where You're Stuck] + [Your Hypothesis on the Issue]**
   Tailored for project or assignment help, this encourages students to explain their project's goals, identify where they're stuck, and share their hypotheses on why the issue is occurring.
   
5. **[Tool or Technology] + [Task You're Trying to Accomplish] + [Challenges Faced]**
   Useful for queries related to specific tools or technologies, this format asks users to name the tool/technology, describe the task they're attempting, and detail the challenges they've encountered.
   
6. **[Debugging Attempts] + [Results of Each Attempt] + [Questions on Next Steps]**
   Focusing on problem-solving processes, this format has users list their debugging attempts, the outcomes of each, and questions about what to do next.
   
7. **[Learning Objective] + [Resources Consulted] + [Remaining Uncertainties]**
   For learning new concepts, users should state their learning goal, list any resources they've already consulted, and mention what uncertainties they still have.
   
8. **[Code Review Request] + [Specific Areas of Concern] + [Goals for Improvement]**
   When seeking a code review, users can outline their request, point out specific areas of concern within their code, and specify their goals for improvement.
   
9. **[Comparison Query] + [Technologies/Concepts Compared] + [Criteria for Comparison]**
   This format is ideal for users making comparisons between technologies or concepts, specifying what's being compared and the criteria for comparison.
   
10. **[Optimization Goal] + [Current Implementation] + [Performance Issues/Constraints]**
    For optimization queries, users should describe their optimization goal, share their current implementation, and detail any performance issues or constraints they're facing.

## Conclusion
Code Mentor is more than just a coding assistant; it's your partner in the learning process. By focusing on understanding, debugging, and applying logic, it aims to build your confidence and skills in programming. Whether you're tackling a tough assignment, learning a new programming language, or debugging an intricate piece of code, Code Mentor is here to guide you every step of the way.

---

Happy coding!

title: How to Build a Blog by Yourself - Part 1: GitHub
content:
## Getting Started: Registering on GitHub

Embarking on the journey to build your own blog? A great first step is to create an account on GitHub. Get started by registering at [GitHub](https://github.com).

> **Note:** Depending on your region, you might need additional tools to bypass internet restrictions for accessing GitHub.

## Setting Up Your GitHub Profile

With your GitHub account ready, here's how to get your profile set up:

1. **Find Your Profile:** Navigate to `https://github.com/[YourGitHubName]`. For instance, my profile is at [https://github.com/shoal-rat](https://github.com/shoal-rat).
2. **Access Repositories:** On your profile page, locate and click on 'Repositories', usually found on the left-hand side.
3. **Create a New Repository:** Click the green 'New' button to begin crafting your blog's repository.

## Creating Your Blog Repository

As you create your blog repository, consider the following:

- **Name Your Repository:** Use the format `[YourName].github.io`, like `shoal-rat.github.io`.
- **Include a README:** Optionally, add a README file to describe your blog or provide essential information.

After these steps, your repository will be all set. However, keep your GitHub page open; we're not done yet! Next, we'll delve into setting up SSH keys for secure access and further steps to customize and deploy your blog using GitHub Pages.

---

Stay tuned for the upcoming guide on these advanced steps!
